strengths: Clear and rigorous technical contribution: Rank-GRPO addresses genuine misalignment in GRPO for rank-structured outputs, with elegant gradient analysis (Eq. 4-7) demonstrating non-causal credit assignment and importance ratio mismatch
Well-motivated problem with practical relevance: Identifies concrete challenges (catalog unawareness, format violations, tail degradation) in applying LLMs to conversational recommendation
Thoughtful two-stage framework: Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline creatively addresses the lack of high-quality in-catalog ranking data using teacher LLM distillation
Strong empirical results: Small models trained with ConvRec-R1 match/exceed GPT-4o and CRAG on REDDIT-V2, with demonstrable improvements especially at tail positions
Comprehensive experimental analysis: Multiple backbones (0.5B, 1B, 3B), on-policy/off-policy settings, training dynamics visualization, and qualitative examples
Excellent reproducibility: Promises to release code, dataset, trained checkpoints, with thorough implementation details (Appendix C)
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Single dataset (REDDIT-V2) and single domain (movies) prevent generalizability claims; no evaluation on e-commerce, books, or other domains despite claiming broad applicability to rank-structured tasks

Missing critical comparison: RecLLM-R1 (Xie et al., 2025), the most directly related concurrent work on GRPO-based CRS, is mentioned but never experimentally compared despite targeting the same problem on the same dataset

Insufficient algorithmic justification: Reward shaping choices (Eq. 8-9) lack rigor—why is Γ = ∞ optimal? Penalties for incomplete/overflow items (ϵu, ϵo) appear ad-hoc; hyperparameters (λ, γ, λw, λb) not ablated

Overlooked practical concerns: Teacher LLM cost (multiple GPT-4o API calls for Remap-Reflect-Adjust) never discussed; figure 6 shows both methods drift from catalog during RL with insufficient investigation of solutions
Missing ablation studies: No isolated evaluation of Remap-Reflect-Adjust components; sensitivity to key hyperparameters (especially Γ) not analyzed
Unexplored cost-efficiency tradeoffs: Dependence on teacher LLM for training data generation undermines efficiency advantages claimed for small models; actual deployment cost not addressed

Inconsistent experimental setup: Requiring title+release year makes comparison with prior work difficult; exact-match parsing success rates not reported; one-month validation-test gap may mask distribution shift
Statistical rigor gaps: Error bars provided but no hypothesis tests; some improvements (Recall@5: 0.005-0.015) may be within error margins; no significance thresholds discussed

strengths: Well-identified problem in applying GRPO to ranking tasks with clear gradient analysis demonstrating misalignment between sequence-level rewards and token-level updates
Practical two-stage framework with well-designed Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline that cleverly leverages teacher LLM knowledge without human annotations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes (0.5B, 1B, 3B), datasets (REDDIT-V2, REDIAL), and training settings (on-policy and off-policy)
Strong empirical results with Llama-3.2-3B variant surpassing GPT-4o and CRAG, showing practical value for smaller models
Detailed ablation studies and training dynamics analysis providing interpretable insights into method behavior
Reproducibility commitment with code, datasets, and trained checkpoints to be released
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of core components: Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline combines existing techniques (semantic similarity, LLM-as-judge, bias learning) heuristically without principled justification; Rank-GRPO itself is a reasonable but incremental algorithmic adaptation

Rank-GRPO lacks theoretical grounding: reward decomposition (Eq. 8-9) is intuitive but arbitrary; geometric mean for importance weighting lacks principled justification; no convergence analysis or optimality guarantees

Narrow evaluation scope: movies only across all datasets; generalization to other domains (e-commerce, video) with different item representations unclear; evaluation limited to ranking metrics without diversity/novelty metrics or human evaluation

Catalog drift problem inadequately addressed: Figure 6 shows in-catalog hit ratio degrades from ~100% to 85-95% during RL training, contradicting SFT grounding; no effective mitigation strategy proposed
Off-policy training exhibits significant performance degradation (5-10% worse metrics, Table 4) limiting practical utility for efficient trajectory reuse; underlying causes not thoroughly analyzed

Incomplete baseline comparisons: no direct comparison with concurrent RecLLM-R1; DPO baselines adapted indirectly via BIGRec potentially unfair; limited engagement with other RL-based recommendation methods

Teacher LLM dependency underexplored: SFT quality strongly depends on teacher model; no analysis of performance with weaker teachers; Reflect step requires multiple teacher calls increasing deployment cost

Extensive hyperparameter tuning with limited sensitivity analysis: Remap-Reflect-Adjust introduces λ, γ, w, b; reward shaping adds Γ, ϵo, ϵu; only ϵo sensitivity provided (Fig. 10); concern about dataset-specific tuning

Evaluation methodology limitations: binary relevance oversimplifies preferences; standard errors substantial (~0.002-0.0035); no statistical significance testing; lack of human evaluation on recommendation quality aspects
Missing computational cost analysis: Remap-Reflect-Adjust requires multiple teacher LLM calls; no wall-clock time comparisons; deployment efficiency vs baselines unknown
